title: p99/p95 tail latency deep dive with Cobalt Dynamics
summary: Redwood AE/SE ran a deep technical session with Cobalt Dynamics infra and ML leads to dissect p95/p99 tail latency sources. Discussed KV cache hit rates, batching windows, streaming vs non-streaming behavior, quantization tradeoffs, and networking/VPC hops. Action items include running a KV-warm benchmark, sharing kernel-level perf traces, and a follow-up test in Cobalt's VPC with a short pilot configuration.
action_items: Maya Patel: Share kernel-level perf traces and current p99 benchmark spreadsheet by 2027-07-14
Rita Alvarez: Provide representative request size distribution and 1 week of production QPS by 2027-07-16
Diego Ramos: Run KV-warm vs cold microbench and share results by 2027-07-19
next_steps: Redwood to share perf traces and recommended batching config
Customer to run KV warm/cold microbench and share results
Schedule follow-up 30-minute pilot kick-off in customer VPC for week of 2027-07-26
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-07-12 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~62 mins | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SE), Evan (CTO Cobalt), Rita (Lead ML), Samir (Infra), Olivia (PM)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we'll focus on the p95/p99 tail latency stuff, Diego and Priya will go deep into runtime and KV stuff. Evan over to you for a quick context.
[00:12] Evan: Yeah hi thanks, want to understand sources of tail latency for our chat assistant. We're seeing p95 around 450ms but p99 spikes to 1.8s on long-turn conversations. Throughput average is fine, qps around 120 sustained.
[00:30] Diego: Ok that's helpful, couple quick clarifying q's — when you say long-turn are we talking >512 tokens or long input prefixes?
[00:38] Rita: Mostly long context, yes — users paste docs, average prompt length 800 tokens, but reply length is usually 80-120 tokens. We stream tokens back to the UI.
[00:48] Priya: Streaming changes the tail pattern because you open a bidi channel and then per-token scheduling matters, also early tokens can be held while KV cache warms.
[00:57] Samir: We're on a VPC setup with TLS termination in our LB, then to Redwood-hosted model endpoints across peered region. There's a couple network hops — LB -> NAT -> Redwood private endpoint. Could that be the issue?
[01:10] Diego: Network hops add jitter, but usually not that large unless there's retransmits or CPU saturation on the LB. We look at two broad categories: model runtime scheduling (GPU queuing, KV cache, batching) and network/infra jitter.
[01:25] Maya: We'll walk through runtime first — Diego, Priya?
[01:29] Diego: Sure. At the runtime level p99 often comes from a combination: cold KV cache misses for long contexts, large dynamic batching window expansion when a big request joins a batch, and rare kernel fallbacks (e.g., fallback to slower matmul kernels if quantization path misses). Example: if most requests are 80 tokens but occasionally you get 800-token prefixes, that request forces more KV loads and causes higher mem bandwidth and occasionally blocks smaller requests if CPU/gpu queues align poorly.
[01:55] Rita: Can you explain KV warm vs cold in plain terms?
[01:58] Diego: Yeah. Warm = KV cache already populated with recent prefix keys so incremental generation is just reading from fast GPU-resident KV; cold = you need to recompute or load KV pages from CPU memory or re-run prefix computation, which is heavy. Warm hits are fast, cold misses cost hundreds of ms to seconds depending on prefix length and model.
[02:13] Priya: And with streaming we often keep the connection open and send tokens as they stream; but the first few tokens might still wait for KV warm or the initial batch scheduling decision. If your batching window is adaptive and tuned for latency, the scheduler may wait a small 10-30ms window to aggregate requests — that helps throughput but increases p95 a bit; p99s usually come from the cold/wide requests or queue head-of-line blocking.
[02:36] Samir: We instrumented our LB and saw some 200-400ms spikes pre-Redwood — mostly TCP retransmits during peak. So part network still.
[02:44] Maya: Helpful to confirm. Let's break down measurable components: client->LB ingress (network jitter), LB->redwood egress + TLS cost, initial prefix compute (CPU/GPU), KV load times (cold vs warm), per-token generation kernel time, batching windows, and final network to client.
[03:05] Olivia: For our SLOs we need p99 < 1s if possible.
[03:09] Diego: Achievable if we address cold KV and avoid big head-of-line blocks. Options: 1) increase proactive KV warming for heavy users, 2) change batching windows / priority scheduling to avoid small important requests being blocked behind a long one, 3) quantization changes — lower precision can reduce kernel latency but may change path.
[03:28] Rita: How does quantization affect p99? We ran 4-bit quantization and saw avg token latency drop 20% but tail seemed worse on long contexts.
[03:36] Priya: That's expected sometimes. Some optimized kernels for 4-bit are super-fast for the main path, but if we hit a code path that doesn't support fused attention or certain KV cache layout, runtime falls back to slower generic kernels — those fallbacks are rare but create large p99 spikes. Also quantized memory layout can increase CPU-GPU transfer complexity on cold path.
[03:55] Diego: Right, so quantization reduces steady-state per-token compute and memory footprint, but if cold KV or prefix handling needs extra CPU copies because the quantized format isn't directly consumable by the fast kernel, you'll see p99 regressions. We mitigate with pre-conversion or ensuring the quant path is complete.
[04:12] Evan: How about batching — you mentioned adaptive windows. We're currently on a target latency of 50ms batching window. 
[04:18] Priya: 50ms is a tight window; it helps p50/p95 but if you have large request variability, that small window can't always absorb the variance. There's two levers: window size and dynamic batching policies (e.g., cap batch size by token cost, or preemptive scheduling for high-priority requests). Larger windows help throughput and can reduce p99 caused by micro-queueing but increase median.
[04:39] Diego: Also consider prefix-aware batching where long-prefix requests are scheduled on separate worker pools or at lower concurrency. Redwood supports model routing by request profile — you can route long-context heavy requests to dedicated nodes so they don't head-of-line block short requests.
[04:53] Samir: That seems promising; we'd rather keep short interactive requests snappy and let bulk docs take longer. Is that config available in hosted? In private?
[05:01] Maya: Yes, both. For Hosted you can use per-route model variants and dispatch policies. For Dedicated/Private you can allocate a separate serving pool. There's a config we can share.
[05:11] Rita: Network hops — is TLS termination and extra NAT expected to add 200ms?
[05:15] Diego: Not usually. TLS handshake only happens on connection setup, not per request if you reuse connections. But if you proxy through multiple proxies with per-request buffering or if you have synchronous verification steps (e.g., auth webhook), that can inflate. TCP retransmits can add 100s ms. Important to check connection reuse and keepalive settings on client LB.
[05:33] Olivia: Our telemetry shows some short-lived clients that open many connections — maybe that's causing renegotiations.
[05:38] Maya: Good call. Keepalive + connection pooling is low-hanging.
[05:42] Rita: On the runtime side, what kernel-level traces can you share?
[05:45] Diego: We can provide a flamegraph-like trace per token: time split across KV read, attention kernels, matmuls, GPU->CPU copies, and scheduler wait. We'll annotate with timestamps to correlate with your LB traces.
[05:58] Evan: Great.
[06:00] [06:00] Diego: Example microcase: 800-token prefix, 120-token gen, quantized 4-bit path. Cold KV miss causes 600ms of prefix recompute; during that period other requests may pile up. If routing not isolated, a single cold heavy request can push p99 above 2s.
[06:22] Priya: Another thing: tokenization cost and detokenize on client side can show up in perceived latency if you measure end-to-end. For p99 strictly at server-side generation call we instrument differently.
[06:33] Rita: For streaming vs non-streaming — we stream but want to know if switching to non-streaming batched response would help tails?
[06:41] Priya: Non-streaming allows the runtime to optimize for full-seq compute (maybe better batching decisions) but delays first token; streaming favors perceived latency (first token arrives sooner) but increases per-token scheduling overhead. Some customers use hybrid: send first token ASAP (stream) then stream rest in micro-batches.
[07:00] Diego: If your p99 is dominated by cold prefix compute, streaming won't hide that initial cost. But if p99 comes from per-token kernel stalls, switching to larger micro-batches can help. It's a measurement question.
[07:13] Rita: Ok can we run A/B: current streaming vs micro-batch non-stream for a sample of traffic?
[07:17] Maya: Yes that's doable, we'll advise test plan.
[07:20] Samir: What about VPC/on-prem routing — if we run private deployment closer to our infra will that reduce p99?
[07:28] Diego: Generally yes. Reducing network hops and colocating reduces jitter and TLS proxying. Private deployment also gives you more control over node isolation for long-prefix workloads. But private has ops overhead.
[07:40] Evan: Ops okay — we have a small infra team. Cost is a factor.
[07:43] Priya: We also discussed proactive KV warming — you can precompute prefixes for known heavy users or recent activity and populate GPU KV so those requests are warm. That costs compute but significantly reduces cold miss p99.
[07:57] Rita: What's the recommended warm window or policy?
[07:59] Diego: Often a time-decay policy with LRU and warm for top N active users. For chat assistants, keep last session prefixes warm for, say, 10-30 minutes depending on memory. We can recommend parameters after we see your qps and unique users distribution.
[08:13] Olivia: Regarding redo/quant — is there a recommended quantization profile that balances p99 and avg latency?
[08:19] Priya: For many models int8 + optimized kernels gives good steady latency without too many fallback paths. 4-bit often needs more careful tuning. If you need the memory reduction, we can test 4-bit but instrument for fallback rates.
[08:33] Diego: Also note that KV layout matters: fused KV layouts allow the GPU kernel to read contiguous memory; if conversion needed on the fly you pay a penalty.
[08:44] Rita: Can Redwood do routing so long contexts go to a separate pool automatically?
[08:48] Maya: Yes — we support routing rules based on token-length, customer-defined metadata, or model variant. We'll share sample configs.
[08:56] Samir: For the follow-up tests we want to run: 1) KV-warm vs cold microbench, 2) streaming vs micro-batch A/B, 3) run in-customer VPC pilot with dedicated short-pref pool.
[09:07] Diego: We'll provide the microbench harness (script + threshold config) so you can reproduce locally. It'll measure p50/p95/p99 and show per-token breakdown.
[09:16] Rita: Ok, timeline?
[09:18] Maya: We'll send traces and configs by EOD 2027-07-14, you run microbench by 7/19, and we reconvene to look at results week of 7/26 and spin up a pilot.
[09:28] Evan: sounds good.
[09:30] [09:30] Diego: Quick note on measurements — ensure you have synchronized clocks (NTP) across LB and app, and capture tcpdump samples on the path when you see spikes. Correlating server-side perf with client network times is critical.
[09:45] Rita: We'll enable more granular logging for the next 48 hours.
[09:49] Priya: One more runtime tip: enable priority preemption for short requests — Redwood runtime can preempt background batch work to push a high-priority short request through. It reduces p99 for interactive. There's a small throughput cost.
[10:04] Olivia: If we preempt, how much throughput hit are we looking at?
[10:07] Diego: Typically a few percent depending on request mix. We'll model it for your profile.
[10:12] Rita: Any red flags about our stack we should fix first?
[10:15] Diego: Connection churn at LB and TCP retransmits — those network issues are quick wins. Then KV warm policy. Then consider route isolation for long contexts, and watch quantization fallback metrics.
[10:27] Maya: Cool, let's recap next steps.
[10:29] Evan: Recap: Redwood shares perf traces + batching config + microbench harness; Cobalt runs KV microbench and shares request distribution; follow-up pilot in VPC week of 7/26.
[10:42] Maya: I'll also include recommended default configs: keepalive 60s, pooling, batching window 25ms (or configurable), priority preemption on for interactive workloads, hot-warm KV policy = 20 mins for active sessions (tunable).
[10:58] Rita: Thank you. Diego, Priya, Maya — appreciate the deep dive.
[11:02] Diego: Thanks everyone.
[11:04] End of meeting.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mislabels and filler words; some proper nouns may be transcribed imperfectly.
